title: The Breakfast Where BioNTech Turned From Cancer to Covid-19
dek: In late January 2020 two cancer researchers in Mainz read the early signs from Wuhan and moved their company onto a vaccine before Germany had a confirmed case.

story.event: Deciding over a weekend to turn a cancer-immunotherapy company towards a coronavirus vaccine (Project Lightspeed)
story.summary: On a Friday in late January 2020 BioNTech's chief executive Uğur Şahin read a Lancet paper on the Wuhan outbreak; that weekend he and his wife and co-founder Özlem Türeci decided to turn their cancer-focused Mainz company towards a coronavirus vaccine, and on the Monday he told a partly sceptical board. Project Lightspeed had 20 candidates by the end of February, partnerships with Fosun and Pfizer followed in March, and the vaccine showed 95% efficacy in a trial of 43,548 people.
paragraphs: On a Friday evening in late January 2020, Uğur Şahin, chief executive of BioNTech, a Mainz company that worked mainly on cancer immunotherapies, read a paper in The Lancet about the new coronavirus in Wuhan. The outbreak, he later said, had been going on for about three weeks. Only a week earlier he and his wife and co-founder, Özlem Türeci, the company's chief medical officer, had presented BioNTech's cancer plans for 2020 in San Francisco.

What they had was not proof. Şahin ran his own projections, which suggested the virus had already spread much further than reported; Türeci later called them "pure mathematics based on our own assumptions." He said he was very worried the outbreak would not stay inside China. Türeci said it was immediately clear to both of them that their mRNA technology could allow a fast response. They talked it through at breakfast. "It was that weekend we already decided we would go for it," she recalled.

On the Monday, Şahin called his board together and said BioNTech would develop a Covid-19 vaccine, with human trials to begin by April. Not everyone agreed. Directors and key staff were about to leave on skiing holidays, and, he told The Wall Street Journal, "Some people thought the situation in China was being hyped up, that it would not affect us." He and Türeci held firm. Scientists cancelled their holidays and were split into separate groups working seven-day weeks on what Şahin called Project Lightspeed, so that one infection could not halt everything. On 28 January, Germany confirmed its first case.

By the end of February the team had 20 candidate vaccines and had chosen four for a trial in Germany. Şahin knew BioNTech could not run a fast trial with tens of thousands of volunteers on its own, so it made a deal with Fosun Pharma for China and, in March, with Pfizer. The decisive trial enrolled 43,548 people, and the vaccine was 95 per cent effective at preventing Covid-19. Britain authorised it on 2 December 2020. The cancer work waited. "Yes, we have lost time," Türeci said later. "But not an entire year."

quote.text: before a thing has given indications of its presence, it is easy to take measures against it; that which is brittle is easily broken; that which is very small is easily dispersed. Action should be taken before a thing has made its appearance; order should be secured before disorder has begun.
quote.source_title: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics, tr. James Legge, Project Gutenberg eBook #216
quote.connection: Laozi's point is about cost: a thing is easiest to meet while it is still small and brittle. The story supplies the part he leaves unsaid, that this is also when acting looks like an overreaction, and when your colleagues are packing for the ski slopes.

reflection: Şahin and Türeci did not know they were right. They had one paper, their own arithmetic and a technology they understood well enough to move quickly. What made the choice workable was that they said it out loud, to each other first and then to a board that partly disagreed, and set a date by which it would be tested.

You will have early signals of your own: a question that keeps coming back, a tiredness that is not lifting, a colleague who has gone quiet. Most will come to nothing. A few are worth meeting while they are still small, and the only way to tell which is to look at one properly instead of carrying it around unexamined.
invitation: Pick one small signal you have noticed this week and keep pushing aside. Write down what you would expect to see by the end of the month if it matters, and put that date in your calendar.

sources.title: Interview: BioNTech founders Özlem Türeci and Ugur Sahin on the vaccine, the pandemic and cancer (Mathias Döpfner)
sources.publisher: Business Insider / WELT, republished by Yahoo News (March 2021)
sources.supports: Şahin read a Lancet publication on a Friday evening; the outbreak had been going on about three weeks; breakfast discussion on 25 January; Şahin's worry that the outbreak would not stay in China; Türeci's 'pure mathematics based on our own assumptions'; 'It was that weekend we already decided we would go for it'; work with the team began on the Monday; Şahin's view that it was not a lone decision and that the supervisory board could be convinced; cancer plans presented a week earlier in San Francisco; Türeci's 'Yes, we have lost time. But not an entire year.'

sources.title: How Pfizer Partner BioNTech Became a Leader in Coronavirus Vaccine Race (Bojan Pancevski and Jared S. Hopkins)
sources.publisher: The Wall Street Journal via Dow Jones Newswires, republished by MarketScreener (22 October 2020)
sources.supports: A new study on a Friday in late January suggesting the virus was more infectious than believed; the following Monday Şahin called his board together and announced a Covid-19 vaccine programme with an April deadline for human trials; directors and key employees about to go on ski holidays pushed back; Şahin's quotation 'Some people thought the situation in China was being hyped up, that it would not affect us'; Şahin and Türeci insisted; staff split into separate groups working seven-day weeks on Project Lightspeed; 20 candidates by the end of February and four chosen for a German trial; deal with Shanghai Fosun Pharmaceutical; Pfizer partnership in March.

sources.title: Vaccine maker recounts breakfast table decision (Frank Jordans)
sources.publisher: Associated Press, republished by Medical Xpress (17 December 2020)
sources.supports: Türeci's account that the decision was made at the breakfast table (she gave the date as 24 January); Şahin alerted the entire company, the supervisory board and the owners and moved resources from cancer therapy to a vaccine; Şahin's statement that BioNTech lacked the capacity to run very quick clinical studies with more than 40,000 volunteers, hence Pfizer; 95% efficacy; UK emergency authorisation on 2 December 2020.

sources.title: From the Lab to the Jab: How BioNTech-Pfizer Won the Vaccine Race
sources.publisher: Agence France-Presse, republished by IndustryWeek (26 December 2020)
sources.supports: Türeci and Şahin decided at breakfast to start work on a vaccine after Şahin read a publication on cases in Wuhan; BioNTech moved its resources from cancer research to the vaccine; Germany confirmed its first case on 28 January 2020; about 95% efficacy; UK approval on 2 December.

sources.title: Husband-and-wife team behind leading vaccine to solve COVID-19 (David Gelles)
sources.publisher: The New York Times, republished by Gulf News (November 2020)
sources.supports: Work began in January after Şahin read an article in The Lancet and became convinced the outbreak would become a pandemic; scientists cancelled holidays to work on Project Lightspeed; Pfizer collaboration agreed in March; the interim result of more than 90% efficacy announced in November 2020.

sources.title: How BioNTech went from a little-known biotech company to creating the Covid vaccine (Katie Brigham)
sources.publisher: CNBC, republished by NBC Chicago (23 October 2021)
sources.supports: BioNTech was mainly a cancer-treatment company before 2020; Şahin concluded in late January that Covid-19 would become a pandemic and he and Türeci agreed to direct most of the company's resources to a vaccine; Türeci's account that it was immediately clear to both of them that their technology could allow a rapid response; earlier Pfizer collaboration on an mRNA flu vaccine since 2018.

sources.title: Safety and Efficacy of the BNT162b2 mRNA Covid-19 Vaccine (Polack et al.)
sources.publisher: New England Journal of Medicine (10 December 2020), via PubMed Central
sources.supports: Peer-reviewed report of the decisive trial (authors include Şahin and Pfizer and BioNTech staff): 43,548 participants randomised; 95% efficacy against laboratory-confirmed Covid-19 (8 cases with vaccine, 162 with placebo).

cross_checks.claim: Şahin read a paper in The Lancet about the Wuhan outbreak in late January 2020 and concluded it would become a pandemic.
Şahin and Türeci made the decision over breakfast at the end of that week, and work with the team started on the Monday.
Staff cancelled holidays to work on what was called Project Lightspeed.
BioNTech partnered with Pfizer in March 2020 because it could not run a large, fast trial alone.
The vaccine was 95% effective in the decisive trial and the UK authorised it on 2 December 2020.

research_notes: Date of the decision: in the AP interview (December 2020) Türeci said she remembered 'the precise day, Jan. 24' when they decided at the breakfast table, and AFP also dates the breakfast decision to 24 January. In the later Döpfner interview (March 2021) Şahin says he read the Lancet paper on the Friday evening (24 January 2020 was a Friday) and the interviewer places the breakfast on 25 January, with Türeci saying 'It was that weekend we already decided'. The WSJ says only 'a Friday in late January'. The story therefore says Friday evening for the reading and 'that weekend' for the decision, and gives no exact date for the breakfast. The WSJ describes the trigger as an emailed study suggesting the virus was more infectious than believed; the NYT and Döpfner name The Lancet; the specific Lancet paper is not identified in the cited sources, so the story does not name it. Efficacy: the NYT piece (November 2020) reports the interim 'more than 90%' announced on 9 November; AFP, AP and the NEJM trial report give the final 95%; the story uses the final peer-reviewed figure. Trial size: Şahin (AP) spoke of 'more than 40,000 volunteers'; NEJM gives 43,548 randomised; the story uses the NEJM figure and 'tens of thousands' for what Şahin anticipated. Headcount: the WSJ's 'about 1,500 staff' describes October 2020, not January, so no January headcount is given. 'Scientists cancelled their holidays' combines the NYT ('cancelled vacations') with the WSJ (staff about to go skiing). Funding: BioNTech was built on private investment (the Strüngmann family office and MIG among others, per AP) and had also sold shares publicly (the NYT mentions its public share sale); 'venture' reflects that private backing. Several founder quotations come from republished copies (Yahoo for Business Insider/WELT, MarketScreener for the WSJ, Medical Xpress for AP, IndustryWeek for AFP, Gulf News for the NYT) because the originals are paywalled or block automated requests; pfizer.com and investors.biontech.de returned 403.
